outcomes.original: Filing step: Request a pre-application meeting with SF Planning Department to confirm the Calle 24 SUD frontage calculation and verify that the project will not exceed the 35% restaurant cap within 300 feet. What to say: Email the current planner or Zoning Administrator to request a pre-application meeting, stating: 'We are proposing a 1,540 sq ft restaurant with no alcohol at 3034 24th St in the Calle 24 SUD. Planning Code § 249.59(d)(1) prohibits a new restaurant where such uses would exceed 35% of commercial frontage within 300 ft. Can Planning confirm the current percentage of restaurant/bar frontage within 300 ft, and whether this project would be permitted under the cap?' Do not file the CUA application or pay the filing fee until Planning confirms in writing that the project is not prohibited by the frontage cap.
outcomes.note: The record identifies the district and code section but does not state what § 249.59(d)(1) requires or contain any text about a 35% frontage cap.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with SF Planning Department, attaching the DBI violation clearance letter and the pre-application meeting notes confirming Calle 24 frontage compliance. What to say: Submit the CUA application online through the Planning Department portal, selecting 'Restaurant (change of use)' as the project type. Describe the concept as a 1,540 sq ft neighborhood-serving restaurant with limited cooking, no alcohol, and standard hours (e.g., 7 AM to 10 PM), emphasizing that it supports the pedestrian-oriented, commercial character of the NCT-24TH-MISSION district and fills a vacant retail space. Attach floor plans, a sample menu, and the DBI clearance letter. Note that the project is not formula retail (if true). The filing fee is typically $3,000–$6,000 depending on construction cost; confirm the current fee schedule with Planning.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Attend the pre-application community meeting and any neighborhood outreach required by Planning, addressing concerns about density, odor, noise and sidewalk maintenance. What to say: Planning may require a neighborhood meeting before scheduling the CUA hearing. Present the concept as a small-scale, food-focused restaurant that will activate a vacant space, explaining the limited cooking (not a full kitchen), no alcohol service, and standard daytime/early evening hours. Address density concerns by noting that the use is principally permitted by right up to 2,500 sq ft (this project is 1,540 sq ft) and that the CU is required only because of the zoning district table and the Mission Alcohol SUD overlay. Commit to the standard conditions (odor control, soundproofing, sidewalk maintenance, garbage inside, community liaison) to demonstrate good-neighbor practices.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Public Health plan check application with SF DPH Environmental Health Branch, submitting floor plans, equipment specifications, a menu, and the finishes schedule. What to say: Apply online through the DPH portal at least 60 days before the target opening date. Describe the concept as a limited-cooking restaurant (e.g., panini press, toaster oven, coffee bar—specify the actual equipment), provide two sets of scaled drawings showing the kitchen layout, hand sinks, three-compartment sink, prep surfaces, walk-in cooler (if any), and restroom facilities. Include interior/exterior photos, a sample menu, and a signed Certified Food Protection Manager certificate. Pay the plan check fee ($828–$2,207 depending on complexity; confirm with DPH). The plans must match the CUA-approved layout and demonstrate compliance with the California Retail Food Code.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the building permit application with SF DBI, routing it to Planning, DPH, PUC (for grease interceptor) and any other required departments. What to say: Submit stamped architectural plans prepared by a California-licensed architect, showing the tenant improvements, finishes, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, and kitchen equipment. On the permit application form, check the box for 'change of use' and note 'CUA approved [Motion No., date]' in the description field. DBI will route the permit to Planning for Section 175 zoning compliance review, to DPH for final plan approval, and to PUC for grease interceptor requirements. Fees are a percentage of construction valuation (typically $800–$15,000); budget 14–120 days for plan review and corrections. Do not begin construction until the permit is issued.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Schedule the DPH pre-opening inspection after construction is substantially complete, and request the health permit to operate after passing the final inspection. What to say: Contact your DPH plan reviewer at least two weeks before the target opening to schedule the pre-opening inspection. Walk the space with the inspector to verify that the built facility matches the approved plans: hand sinks in place with hot water, three-compartment sink, smooth and sealed surfaces, adequate ventilation, certified food manager on site, and all equipment installed per specifications. Correct any deficiencies immediately. Once the facility passes the final inspection, DPH will issue the health permit to operate ($470 application fee, $0 annual license fee for 2026–28). You cannot serve food to the public until the permit is issued.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $3,100 to $15,000. Notes: The day and cost ranges cover the three approvals in the entitlement path: Conditional Use Authorization (Planning Commission), health permit to operate (DPH), and building permit with change of use (DBI). The CUA is the long pole: 120–300 days from filing to Commission approval, per the catalog entry for a conditional use authorization in San Francisco, and comparable restaurant CUAs in this district took 20–408 days to approval (N = 8 approved cases). Government costs include the CUA filing fee ($3,100–$15,000 depending on construction cost, with potential First Year Free fee waiver for new storefront businesses), the health plan check fee ($828–$2,207), the health permit application fee ($470), and the building permit fee ($800–$15,000 as a percentage of construction valuation). These are times and costs to obtain the approvals when they are granted; they do not account for the scenario where the Calle 24 frontage cap prohibits the project or where the applicant withdraws. The timeline assumes no appeals and that the DBI violations from the 2009 fire damage have been abated before filing begins. Add 60–120 days if the CUA is appealed to the Board of Supervisors. The building permit review (14–120 days) and health permit issuance (14–45 days) run after the CUA is approved, so the total time from first filing to opening is roughly 150–465 days, not including pre-application research or construction time.
